source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization with Failure Trajectories: A Tree-based Approach to Elicit Optimal Policy in Strong Models
source.authors: Rui-Meng Ye; Zihan Wang; Yang Xiao; Zi-Nan Ling; Man-Ling Li; Bo Hui

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong learning on interactive agent tasks, but uses trajectory-tree DPO and MCTS and task reward rather than the original label-fine-tuning procedure and PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports task rewards and success rates for weak and strong models, training variants, task settings, and model sizes. It does not calculate PGR. It also reports comparisons among other baselines; those comparator results are not entered as rows unless they directly help establish the weak-supervisor comparison or method/size results.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether weak-to-strong generalization holds in a new setting: multi-step LLM-agent tasks (WebShop, ScienceWorld, AlfWorld). A strong model is trained on trajectories explored by a weaker SFT model and compared with the weak model, a strong SFT model and a ceiling model. It changes the recipe (trajectory trees, TreeDPO, MCTS), uses task reward instead of PGR, and its supervision includes ground-truth environment scores G(e), which are used to pair and select weak trajectories.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that W2SG holds for interactive agent tasks: strong models trained on weak-model success and failure trajectories beat the weak SFT model. MCTS-based W2SG even beats the expert-trained strong SFT model. They claim formal guarantees for TreeDPO and say the effect generalizes across families and sizes. They acknowledge that weak-model misalignment could transfer but do not test it.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fine-tuning the strong model directly on weak-produced discrete labels, the study has a fine-tuned weak agent explore environments, builds trajectory trees, and trains the strong model with tree-structured DPO preferences or MCTS-selected trajectories. The paper reports task reward/success, not PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance changes with training method (TreeDPO, MCTS, unstructured DPO), β, trajectory-tree breadth/count, weak-model size, model family, and task.
record.peer_reviewed: ICLR 2026 (paper states it was published as a conference paper)
record.problems: PGR is not calculated. The principal results use task-specific reward and success measures, and the paper does not provide all weak-supervisor scores for its larger-model tables. Reported p-values are overall comparisons, not attached to individual task rows. The theory depends on substantive assumptions, including an assumed link between preference loss and task performance.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Table 1 strong-SFT, ETO, Best-of-N, and ceiling-model results as comparator-only outcomes; omitted standalone weak/SFT entries where they only supply baselines already recorded in relevant rows. Table 6 weak-model scores are cited in notes for the supervisor-size comparison, rather than added as separate intervention rows.

untested.parts: Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors and loss variants. No PGR is reported, and no naive SFT-on-weak-trajectories baseline is given; the only naive W2S comparator is unstructured DPO in Table 5 (one model, one task).
Chess, reward modelling, and representation-based predictors of PGR.
All of V4. Imitation of weak errors is mentioned only as a limitation, not tested.
All of V6. The experiments are text-only agents.
The original discrete-label fine-tuning recipe and the PGR metric itself.

missing.what: The paper's own PGR-like claim that weak supervision recovers 'up to 39.4%' of ceiling performance. This is unclear and does not match Table 1. Also, the 'maximum of 4.3%' gain over the weak SFT model conflicts with Table 1 (47.1→53.2).
Weak-supervisor scores for the Llama2-13B→Llama3-8B setting, available from Table 1 (Llama-2-13b+SFT: 51.0/53.6/51.5). Rows r11–r16 do not use them.
Significance tests: t-tests over 5 seeds, p=0.0003 (TreeDPO vs strong SFT) and p=0.0001 (MCTS vs strong SFT). These are pooled, not per task.

record.verdict_notes: Main caveat: the supervision is not purely weak. Weak trajectories are scored by the environment's ground-truth reward G(e), which is used to form TreeDPO pairs and to drive MCTS selection, so the student receives oracle outcome information. This likely explains why students often exceed even the expert-trained strong SFT model (implied PGR >1 against strong SFT). Against the paper's Ceiling Model, implied PGRs for Llama2-13B are about 0.54–0.90 (TreeDPO) and 0.88–>1 (MCTS). Table 8 (70B) does not state the weak supervisor. Table 3's TreeDPO β=0.1 value (54.9) conflicts with Table 1 (55.4). Table 1's strong-SFT and Ceiling values are needed to compute PGR and should be added as rows, even though rows_left_out declares them.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not compute PGR or test the original discrete-label fine-tuning recipe; its evidence is from interactive trajectories and task scores.
Tests TreeDPO, MCTS, unstructured preference pairs, and selected parameter/tree-breadth choices; does not test auxiliary confidence loss or ensembling weak supervisors, or report PGR.
Tests several model sizes/families and interactive tasks. It does not test reward modelling or chess, nor predictors based on representations.
No direct experiment on strong-student exploitation of weak-supervisor blind spots, correlated errors, or distribution-shift effects on W2SG.
Theoretical discussion is for TreeDPO under stated assumptions; it does not establish a general guarantee for arbitrary weak-to-strong training.
No vision-model experiment. AlfWorld is described as cross-modal, but the reported agent experiments use text interactions.

rows.operation_detail: Theoretical performance guarantee for TreeDPO under the paper's assumptions.

conditions.value: strong-model expressivity and superior policy; weak-model coverage and tree richness; informative tree-derived preferences

rows.value: Theorem 1 states a bound involving the improvement margin, KL/complexity terms, and preference-pair count Np; it says outperforming the SFT-strong baseline requires a sufficiently large improvement margin relative to the estimation-error/complexity term.

rows.check: The theorem's comparator is the strong SFT model, not the weak supervisor. The key loss-to-performance link (Eq. 13) is posited, not derived.
